12.20. The Sarmatians ride about in the open plains. And to keep these too from the Danube, through the same Lentulus, was enough. They have nothing but snows and frosts and woods. So great is their barbarism that they do not even understand peace.
12.21. Germany too—would that he had not thought it worth so much to conquer! It was lost more disgracefully than it was gloriously acquired.

12.22. But since he knew that his father Gaius Caesar had twice crossed the Rhine by a bridge and sought war, in his honour he had longed to make it a province; and it had been done, had the barbarians been able to bear our vices as well as our commands.

12.23. Drusus, sent into that province, first subdued the Usipetes, then overran the Tencteri and the Catti. For he adorned a certain raised mound, in the fashion of a trophy, with the spoils and insignia of the Marcomanni.

12.24. Then he attacked at once the most powerful nations, the Cherusci, the Suebi, and the Sicambri, who, having crucified twenty centurions, had taken up the war as though by this oath, with so sure a hope of victory that they divided the plunder beforehand by agreement. The Cherusci chose the horses,
12.25. the Suebi the gold and silver, the Sicambri the captives; but all turned out the reverse. For Drusus, victorious, divided and sold their horses, herds, torques, and themselves as plunder;

12.26. and besides, for the protection of the province, he disposed garrisons and watch-posts everywhere, along the river Meuse, along the Elbe, along the Weser. On the bank of the Rhine indeed he set up more than fifty forts. Borma and Gesoriacum he joined by bridges and secured with fleets.

12.27. The Hercynian forest, hated and inaccessible until that time, he opened up. In short, there was such peace in Germany that the men seemed changed, the land other, the very sky milder and softer than it was wont.
12.28. In short, not through flattery but from his deserts, that bravest of young men having died there, he himself, what never elsewhere, gave a surname from the province to the senate.
12.29. But it is harder to hold provinces than to make them;

12.30. by strength they are won, by justice retained. And so that joy was brief. For the Germans had been conquered rather than tamed, and under the general Drusus they admired our manners rather than our arms;

12.31. after he died, they began to hate the lust and pride of Quintilius Varus no less than his cruelty. He dared to hold an assize, and had issued an edict to the Catti, as though he could restrain the violence of barbarians by the rods of a lictor and the voice of a herald.
12.32. But they, who had long grieved that their swords were rusted over and their horses idle, as soon as they saw the togas and laws more savage than arms,
12.33. under the leadership of Arminius take up arms; while meanwhile Varus had such confidence in peace that he was not even moved by the conspiracy betrayed through Segestes, one of the chiefs.
12.34. And so, attacking him unawares, unprovided and fearing nothing of the kind, when he—O security—was summoning men to the tribunal, they invade from every side; the camp is seized,
12.35. three legions are overwhelmed. Varus followed both the fate and the spirit of Paulus on the same day as the Cannensian disaster.
12.36. Nothing was bloodier than that slaughter through the marshes and woods, nothing more intolerable than the insults of the barbarians, especially against the pleaders of causes.

12.37. The eyes of some they cut off, the hands of others; of one the mouth was sewn up, the tongue being first cut out, which the barbarian, holding in his hand, said at last, "Viper, you have ceased to hiss."

12.38. The body too of the consul himself, which the loyalty of the soldiers had hidden in the ground, was dug up. The standards and two eagles the barbarians still possess; the third the standard-bearer, before he came into the enemy's hands, tore off, and, carrying it hidden in the recesses of his belt, lay hidden thus in the bloody marsh. By this disaster it came about that the empire, which had not stopped on the shore of the Ocean, stopped on the bank of the river Rhine.

12.40. These things toward the north: beneath the south there was tumult rather than war. The Musulami and Gaetuli, dwellers by the Syrtes, he checked under the leadership of Cossus; whence that surname Gaeticus, wider than the victory itself.
12.41. The Marmaridae and Garamantes he gave to Quirinius to be subdued. He too could have returned Marmaricus, but was more modest in valuing his victory.

12.42. Toward the east there was more trouble with the Armenians. Thither he sent one of the Caesars, his grandsons. Both were short-lived by fate, but the one ingloriously. For at Massilia Lucius is released by disease, in Syria Gaius died of a wound, when he was recovering into his power Armenia as it was withdrawing itself to the Parthians.

12.43. The Armenians, King Tigranes being conquered, Pompey had accustomed to this one kind of servitude, that they should receive their governors from us. The right, then, interrupted, was through him recovered, not without blood,

12.44. nor yet with much fighting. For Dones, whom the king had set over Artageris, attacking by feigned betrayal the man intent upon a paper, which he himself had handed him as containing the accounts of the treasures, suddenly, with drawn steel, fell upon him. And then indeed Caesar was for the time recovered from his wound, but * * *. For the rest, the barbarian, overwhelmed on every side by the hostile army, by the sword and the pyre into which, struck, he threw himself, gave satisfaction to Caesar, even then surviving.

12.46. In the west almost all Spain was at peace, save that which, clinging to the rocks of the Pyrenees as it ends, the nearer Ocean washes. Here two most powerful nations, the Cantabri and the Astures, lived exempt from empire.

12.47. The spirit of the Cantabri was both the earlier and the fiercer and the more stubborn in rebelling, who, not content to defend their own liberty, tried also to lord it over their neighbours, and wearied the Vaccaei and the Turmogi and the Autrigones

12.48. with frequent incursions. Against these, then, because it was announced that they were acting too violently, an expedition was not entrusted but undertaken. He himself came to Segisama, pitched camp, then, his army in three parts embracing the whole of Cantabria, hemmed in the savage race, in the manner of beasts, as it were by a kind of net.

12.49. Nor was there rest from the Ocean, when even the rear of the enemy was cut down by a hostile fleet. First there was fighting against the Cantabri beneath the walls of Bergida. Thence at once flight into the loftiest Mount Vindius, whither they had believed that the seas of the Ocean would sooner climb than the arms of Rome.

12.50. Thirdly the town of Aracelium resisted with great force; yet it was taken. Last of all was the siege of Mount Medullius, which, encompassed by a continuous ditch of eighteen miles, the Roman approaching on every side at once, after the barbarians see the extremity, vying with one another by fire, by steel, amid their feasts, and by poison, which there is commonly pressed from the yew, anticipated death, and the greater part rescued themselves from a captivity which to those till then untamed seemed heavier than death.
12.51. These things Caesar, wintering in the maritime parts of Tarraco, received through his legates Antistius and Furnius and through Agrippa.
12.52. Soon he himself, being present, led some down from the mountains, bound others by hostages, sold others under the crown by the right of war.
12.53. The matter seemed to the senate worthy of a laurel, worthy of a triumphal car; but Caesar was now so great that he disdained to be increased by a triumph.

12.54. The Astures at that time had come down with a vast column from the snowy mountains. Nor did this onset seem rashly undertaken by the barbarians; but, their camp being pitched by the river Astura, their column being divided into three parts, they prepared to attack at once three camps of the Romans.
12.55. And the struggle would have been doubtful and bloody and—would it had been with mutual slaughter—with men so brave,

12.56. so sudden, so coming with counsel, had not the Brigaecini betrayed them, by whom, forewarned, Carisius came up with his army. To have overwhelmed their counsels was as good as a victory, yet even so the contest was not bloodless.

12.57. The remnants of the routed army the most powerful city Lancia received, where there was such a struggle over the place that, when torches were demanded for the captured city, the leader scarcely obtained pardon, that it should rather stand as a monument of the Roman victory than be burned.

12.59. This was the end of Augustus's warlike contests, and the same the end of Spain's rebelling. There followed soon a sure faith and an eternal peace, both from the temper of the people themselves, more ready for the arts of peace, and from the counsel of Caesar, who, fearing the confidence of the mountains into which they withdrew, ordered them to inhabit and dwell in his own camp,

12.60. because it was on the plain; there to hold the council of the nation, that to be observed as the capital. The nature of the region favoured the counsel; for round about it is all gold-bearing and rich in malachite and vermilion and other colours. And so he ordered the soil to be worked. So the Astures, striving in the deep for their own wealth and riches, while they seek them for others, began to know them.

12.61. All the nations to the west and south being pacified, to the north also, that is, within the Rhine and the Danube, and to the east within the Cyrus and the Euphrates, those too who remained exempt from empire yet felt the greatness and revered the Roman people, victor of nations.

12.62. For both the Scythians sent envoys and the Sarmatians seeking friendship. The Seres too and the Indians who dwell beneath the very sun, bringing elephants among their gifts with gems and pearls, charged nothing more than the length of the way—they had filled four years; and the very colour of the men confessed that they came from another sky.
12.63. The Parthians too, as though they repented of victory, of their own accord brought back the standards taken in the Crassian disaster.

12.64. So everywhere there was a sure and continual peace or compact of the whole human race, and at last Caesar Augustus dared, in the seven-hundredth year from the founding of the city, to close the double Janus, shut before him twice, under King Numa and when Carthage was first conquered.

12.65. Hence, turning to peace, he restrained with grave and severe laws an age prone to all vices and flowing into luxury; for which so many great deeds he was called perpetual imperator and father of his country.

12.66. It was debated too in the senate whether, because he had founded the empire, he should be called Romulus; but the name of Augustus seemed more holy and reverend, so that, even while he dwells on earth, by his very name and title he should be consecrated.
